results.title: AI Computing Rental Prices Face Downward Pressure as Supply Expands, Goldman Sachs Warns | Gate News
highlights:
According to Goldman Sachs analysis, AI computing rental prices face significant downward pressure as datacenter supply expands. Short-term spot rental rates for AI computing capacity reached $40–50 billion per gigawatt annually, more than double the $20–30 billion per gigawatt for long-term contracts, reflecting temporary supply scarcity. Goldman Sachs warned that as major cloud providers' self-built datacenters come online, the spot market's scarcity premium may diminish, pressuring revenue for supercomputing cloud providers.

SpaceX, Nebius, and CoreWeave currently charge $40–50 billion per gigawatt for near-term contracts, according to recent disclosures. Goldman Sachs estimates self-built capacity requires only $11.6 billion per gigawatt annually to achieve 15% return on invested capital, suggesting current rental rates are 2–4 times above threshold levels. SpaceX's AI capacity is projected to expand from 1.4 gigawatts in mid-2026 to 10.6 gigawatts by end-2028, accelerating the shift in supply dynamics.

results.title: The AI Boom Has Stoked a Gold Rush for Compute Power | Technology for Oct. 11 - WSJ
highlights:
The AI boom has become so frothy that for the top companies, securing computing power can be a much bigger stress than raising capital.

There’s an ongoing desperate scramble to find available AI chips and data-center infrastructure from cloud providers, neoclouds and a number of upstart marketplaces offering quick access to computing power. It’s redrawing tech’s battle lines, determining who can compete and which investors can win the best deals.

Inside the largest tech companies, top AI researchers are feuding over which projects should take priority if computing power is finite. At the same time, former rivals like Anthropic and SpaceX AI are forming new alliances in an effort to secure more processing.

Many startup leaders are concerned that smaller companies trying to compete with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic—already at a disadvantage in a David-vs.-Goliath dynamic—are being crippled by their struggle to source computing contracts.

results.title: State of the GPU Rental Market, October 2026 | FastGPU
highlights:
In the week to October 10, NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs and the H200 were the hardest to rent on demand. The providers that publish stock information had a B300 rentable in 75% of their stock checks, a B200 in 76% and an H200 in 76%, while 15 of the 24 GPUs with enough signal to measure were rentable in every check. Over the same days, the cheapest posted B200 did not move at all: it stood at $3.69/hr in each of the last 7 daily fixings, set by the same provider every day, while the typical provider's price rose. The GPU rental market in October 2026 behaves like two markets: a tight one for Blackwell and H200, priced in a narrow band and getting dearer, and a loose one for older cards that are always in stock, priced far apart and noisy at the floor.

...

## Key findings

- Blackwell and H200 are scarce on demand. In the week to October 10, the B300 was rentable in 75% of stock checks, the B200 in 76%, the H200 in 76%, and the RTX PRO 6000 in 79%, while 15 GPUs were rentable in 100% of checks.
- The H100 SXM had the week's biggest drop. Its rentable share fell from 100% to 87% week on week (it was back at 100% on October 10), and all 8 of its confirmed list-price changes in the last 60 days were rises.
- The floor holds while list prices climb. The price index stands at 99.1, 0.9% below its August base, yet the price-change log holds 81 rises against 4 cuts. The B300's median rose from $8.50 to $9.51 in a week while its floor did not move.
- Rent runs far above the chip's book cost. An H100 SXM rents for a median $3.95/hr; written off over CoreWeave's 6-year schedule, the chip costs $0.48 per GPU-hour and pays for itself in 8.7 months rented around the clock.
- The best GPU per dollar depends on which price you use. At each GPU's floor, the MI355X buys the most benchmarked throughput per rented dollar in one MLPerf® Inference v6.1 scenario, 5,343 tokens/s per $/hr (derived, unverified); at the median price, the B200, B300, GB200 and MI300X are close to a tie.

...

Older cards are not the constraint. The RTX 4090, RTX 5090, L40S, L4, A100 40GB and V100 were all rentable in 100% of checks. For these GPUs a buyer's questions are price and host quality. For the newest GPUs the order reverses: expect roughly one attempt in four to find nothing at a given provider, and keep a second provider or a fallback GPU ready. A posted in-stock flag also says one more GPU could be rented, not how many; for a full node or a cluster, the availability that matters is a capacity holder's answer to a specific request, which is what the cluster quote desk collects. Our guide to where to rent GPUs covers how providers differ beyond price and stock.

...

The price-change log, which records confirmed moves in providers' own posted rates and leaves out marketplace hosts, tells a different story. Of its 85 entries, 81 are rises and 4 are cuts. In the 60-day window to October 10, every confirmed list-price change for the four flagship data-center GPUs was a rise: 8 for the H100 SXM across 5 providers, with a median step of 14.3%; 6 for the H200 (median step 17.5%); 7 for the B200 ( 17.7%, or $1.20 per GPU-hour); and 6 for the B300 ( 10.4%). One recorded example: RunPod's on-demand B200 went from $6.79 to $7.99 per GPU-hour on October 8. FastGPU's monthly State of GPU prices for September counted 15 posted prices that rose and 0 that fell.

...

The medians show that climb directly. Between the fixings of October 5 and October 11, the B300's on-demand median across 10 providers outside the hyperscalers rose from $8.50 to $9.51 per GPU-hour ($9.51 / $8.50 = 1.119, a rise of about 12%), and the B200's from $6.89 to $7.13, while both floors stayed exactly where they were. The H100 SXM median held at $3.95. A week of fixings is a short record and nothing here is a forecast, but the budgeting lesson is plain: a floor that does not move is not evidence that prices are stable. Budget from the median, and check the price-change log for the providers you use.

...

Spread runs the other way from scarcity. The GPUs that are hardest to rent are priced in the tightest band: the B200's 90th-percentile provider charges $8.59 and its 10th-percentile provider $5.10, across 12 providers. For the A100 80GB the same ratio is 3.53x ( $3.52 against $1.00 across 15 providers). Provider choice is worth more the older the GPU: on an A100 80GB, moving from the 90th-percentile provider to the 10th cuts the hourly rate by about 72% (1 - $1.00 / $3.52 = 0.72), while on a B200 the binding question is whether anyone has stock. Our map of the cheapest cloud GPUs explains where the low-end offers come from and what they trade away.

Three prices for the same GPU-hour

Floor, on-demand median outside the hyperscalers, and hyperscaler median, daily fixing of Oct 11, 2026

| Gpu | Floor | On-demand median | Hyperscaler median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A100 80GB | $0.87 | $1.93 | $3.55 |
| H100 SXM | $1.68 | $3.95 | $6.88 |
| H200 | $2.69 | $4.54 | $10.00 |
| B200 | $3.69 | $7.13 | $14.00 |
| B300 | $4.89 | $9.51 | $16.40 |

Source: FastGPU daily fixings, Oct 11, 2026, CC BY 4.0

The basis is the gap between the price a contract follows and the price you pay. It matters now because CME Group's exchange NYMEX has asked the CFTC to approve two cash-settled futures contracts on GPU rental prices, one for the H100 and one for the B200, settling on the monthly average of Silicon Data's H100 rental index and its B200 counterpart - NYMEX Submission No. 26-370. Each contract covers 730 GPU-hours, one GPU for an average month. FastGPU does not reproduce the index values, which belong to their publisher; its own fixings show how far apart the prices a buyer might actually pay sit. In the October 11 fixing, the H100 SXM's on-demand median outside the hyperscalers was $2.27 above the floor and the hyperscaler median another $2.93 above that. For the B200 the two gaps were $3.44 and $6.87. A hyperscaler customer paying $6.88 for an H100 SXM is paying about four times the $1.68 floor ($6.88 / $1.68 = 4.1).

...

The page sets those schedules against Epoch AI's estimate of what each chip cost its buyer and the GPU's median posted on-demand price outside the hyperscalers. ... For the

...

The striking pattern is how uniform payback is. Across seven GPUs released between 2020 and 2025, from NVIDIA and AMD, the chip pays back at the median posted price within 6.2 to 8.7 months rented around the clock. Posted rent appears to be set roughly in proportion to what the chip cost, whatever its age. On CoreWeave's schedule, renting 12% of the hours at the median covers an H100 SXM chip, and 9% covers a B300. At an illustrative 60% of hours rented, a labelled assumption rather than a measurement, H100 SXM payback stretches to 14.5 months. How much of the year a GPU actually earns decides the economics, a point our analysis of what it costs to run a model on your own GPU makes from the renter's side.

results.title: a16z chart: GPU rental prices hold firm while token prices fall, a Jevons-style pattern | Dealroom News
highlights: Nathan LeClaire flagged an a16z Growth chart, compiled by Citadel Securities from Ornn, Silicon Data and Bloomberg data as of August 2026, that tracks the H100 GPU rental price against a token-price expenditure index. In late spring the two moved down together, but from July token prices kept falling, with the index dropping from roughly 1.6 to about 1.0, while the H100 rental price stayed at around $2.7 an hour. The chart is titled "Jevons: Compute Prices Rise As Token Prices Fall": cheaper tokens appear to be lifting demand for compute rather than easing it. Theo (t3.gg) quote-posted it with the comment "Called it".

results.title: The machine rents high. The product keeps getting cheaper. · ThinkPattern
highlights:
The entire AI buildout was financed on one assumption — that compute stays scarce-priced long enough for the product to grow into the bill — and this year the price of the machine and the price of the product finally pulled apart.

...

The two figures do not look like an argument. They are the argument, set down in a term sheet before any market opened, and everything else this year is that gap moving out into the world. The gap matters because, for a rented-out chip, the value of the collateral and the revenue that pays the debt are the same variable. A GPU is worth what it can earn in rent. Rent is set by how scarce compute is. So a lender who writes "this asset depreciates in four years" and a borrower who writes "it lasts a decade" are not arguing about hardware. They are arguing about how long today's prices hold — which means the underwriting is the assumption about the shortage. The providers' own paper shows the mechanism running in both directions. CoreWeave has drawn roughly $35 billion of asset-level debt against a $104.2 billion contracted backlog, debt secured by revenue that is itself a promise to keep renting compute at today's rates. And the company's filings flag the downside in a single clause: margin compression "if the supply of compute normalizes." [2] On the input side, the shortage is real and measured. Global data center supply reached 8.9 gigawatts operational last year against 21.1 gigawatts of demand, a 12-gigawatt deficit. [3] The memory every AI chip needs is expected to stay short through 2028, and possibly to 2030. [4] These are the numbers that make "a decade of scarcity" feel like a safe bet, and they are the numbers Nvidia is lending against. Then, in one week in May, the other half of the bet moved. On May 23, DeepSeek made its flagship model's 75 percent price cut permanent — on Huawei processors, not Nvidia's — and priced the result 12 to 19 times cheaper than GPT-5.5 or Claude Opus 4.7 for an equivalent task. [5]

...

The arithmetic of the pinch is not subtle. Morgan Stanley ran a fully optimized data center on the newest Nvidia chips and found it would cost about $25 billion a year to rent while producing $23 billion of output — and that its 31 percent return on invested capital holds only if the hourly price stays at $8.50. [6] Every model priced below that is a model eating the margin the debt was written against. The credit market has begun to vote, in the clipped, dry way credit markets do. By the second quarter, the hyperscalers' combined capital spending had crossed above their combined operating cash flow; the buildout is now funded off the balance sheet rather than the income statement. [7] Alphabet posted its first negative free cash flow on record, and Meta's quarterly figure fell 91 percent. [8] In Texas, the power futures that price the physical input to all this have already cooled — the forward market for electricity no longer believes the most extreme data center projections. [9] The people who underwrite the debt say it plainly. The cost of insuring a hyperscaler's bonds against default has widened about 60 basis points relative to a bank's since October 2025. [10] Apollo's chief economist describes what is being repriced in one sentence.

...

What realized AI revenue looks like at one of the world's largest IT firms is a useful yardstick: Tata Consultancy Services, up 15 percent on profit, reported annualized AI revenue of $3.1 billion — real, billed money, and orders of magnitude smaller than what is being spent on the buildout. [14] The bull case needs no fence around it; it is one horn of the same fork, and it sharpens rather than dissolves the contradiction. The shortage half is genuine, and the people holding the chips say so — Nebius reports demand still outstripping supply. [15] The hedge fund manager Gavin Baker points to how long the scarcity has already outlived the skeptics.

...

That is the shortage winning. It is exactly what makes the other number — the product's price — so strange. If compute is this scarce, the output ought to cost more, not less. DeepSeek did not wait for the shortage to clear. The industry's own executives concede the stakes without much prompting. Vesora's Sandra Rivera argues the spending is finally crossing over from training to inference, with enterprise demand unbroken; but she adds the caveat herself.

...

The argument is about to acquire instruments. Later this year, the first futures markets on chip-rental prices arrive — Silicon Data with CME Group, Ornn with Intercontinental Exchange, a Bermuda exchange, and ETFs already filed to track the contracts. [16] [17] For the first time, what a rented GPU will be worth next year becomes a price you can look up rather than a term you negotiate. That is the fork, held open rather than resolved. If rents normalize, the providers' own filings have already conceded what comes next: margin compression. If rents hold, the bill lands on a revenue base that, on today's billed numbers, is still almost entirely a projection. One answer is already written into a depreciation schedule. The other is already written into a price cut. The market simply has not had to choose between them yet.

results.title: Nvidia GPU Rentals Are Booming—but More Providers Don’t Guarantee More Capacity | Answer | Studio Global AI
highlights:
The market for renting Nvidia GPUs is expanding beyond the biggest cloud providers. SemiAnalysis counted 323 Nvidia GPU providers in September, up from 209 less than 11 months earlier; Nvidia, meanwhile, forecast $108 billion in revenue for its October quarter, an 89% year-over-year increase. Those figures point to a fast-growing market—but they don’t tell buyers whether a particular provider can deliver the right GPUs, in the required configuration, when they need them. 2

...

A provider count measures the number of suppliers, not the amount of capacity available for a particular job. Buyers still need to verify the GPU generation, cluster size, configuration, timing and contractual terms they can actually obtain. The reported growth in providers is not, by itself, evidence that large interconnected clusters are immediately available. 2

Pricing benchmarks can add context, but they answer a different question. Ornn’s index reported a settled, transaction-based B200 rental benchmark of $7.53 per GPU-hour on October 10, 2026. That is a dated price reference—not proof that a specific buyer can access a particular cluster, or that prices more than doubled since March. 19

...

Reported SpaceX agreements illustrate that some GPU arrangements are measured in substantial monthly commitments, rather than small, short-term rentals. Anthropic reportedly agreed to pay SpaceX $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 for roughly 325,000 Nvidia GPUs. 7

A separate report says Google will pay $920 million per month from October 2026 through June 2029 for access to roughly 110,000 GPUs, along with CPUs, memory and related components. 13 The reported agreements show large buyers securing compute through another operator; they do not establish how readily smaller buyers can find capacity or what terms are typical across neoclouds.

results.title: AI Keeps Getting Cheaper, but GPU Rental Prices Won't Budge: Inside a16z's Analysis | Promptating
highlights:
a16z argues that as AI gets cheaper to use, compute demand is going up rather than down. With rental prices holding even for older GPUs, the open question is whether that extra demand sticks.

...

- a16z finds that falling AI usage costs and rising compute demand are occurring together.
- H100 rental prices have held steady or risen, and A100 prices were at or above start-of-year levels at the time of observation.
- As of April 2026, roughly 2% of US households pay for an AI service.

In “State of Markets II,” a market analysis report published on September 30, the venture firm a16z argued that falling AI usage costs and rising compute demand are happening at the same time. The price of tokens—the small chunks of text that serve as the billing unit for what goes into an AI model and what comes back out—keeps dropping, yet rental prices for the GPUs that run those models are holding steady or climbing.

...

The report’s central point is that total compute demand can grow even when the cost of a given unit of AI work falls. a16z’s reading is that cheaper AI drives more usage, and that demand is growing faster than costs are coming down. What users pay to use AI and what service operators pay to rent compute are moving in opposite directions.

In an October 11 report, The Decoder framed this as the “Jevons paradox”: when efficiency gains lower the cost of using a resource, consumption rises and overall demand ends up larger. Citing a16z’s data, the outlet said rental prices for H100 GPUs are holding steady or rising. The implication is that cheaper AI translates into stronger demand for hardware.

Rental prices for older GPUs were another point the report highlighted. There had been concern that rental rates for previous-generation hardware would slide over time. a16z said that at the time of observation, A100 rental prices were at or above where they stood at the start of the year. The report cited both rising rental prices for newer-generation GPUs and steady prices for older hardware as evidence of compute demand.

results.title: Token prices are collapsing, and yet GPU rental prices barely move. I think this chart explains why. | Rubén Domínguez Ibar
highlights:
Token prices are collapsing, and yet GPU rental prices barely move. I think this chart explains why.

It comes from a16z Growth and compiles Ornn, Silicon Data and Bloomberg data through August 2026. It plots H100 rental price against an index of token price spending. For most of the spring both lines rose and fell together.

Then in July they split. The token index keeps sliding toward its lows, while H100 rental stays steady around $2.70 an hour.

My read: cheaper tokens are creating more demand than they free up, so compute stays scarce. That's Jevons paradox applied to AI, and it could mean the GPU squeeze lasts longer than people expect. I may be wrong if supply catches up faster.

results.title: Compute Becomes Hard Currency in Silicon Valley's AI Race | AI News Feed
highlights:
Silicon Valley's artificial intelligence race is increasingly being decided by who controls access to computing power, according to QbitAI. The report said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei approached rival Meta for GPU capacity, was rebuffed, and SpaceX profited by reselling Nvidia GPU capacity to Anthropic. The episode has reshaped alliances among model developers, cloud providers, investors and startups, with compute treated as the industry's hard currency.

...

Anthropic's compute needs have grown so large that it has turned to outside suppliers. In May, an agreement with SpaceX was to deliver more than 300 megawatts of new capacity that month, involving 220,000 Nvidia GPUs, and raise usage limits for Claude Code and API, according to the report. The goal was to use more backend compute to serve front-end users: more compute, stronger models and better user retention. Competition is now running on two tracks: product-level competition for users and developers, and infrastructure-level cooperation with whoever can supply resources in time.

Smaller AI startups face a sharper squeeze. They cannot build their own data centers and have relied on flexible, on-demand GPU rentals from cloud platforms such as AWS. As leading AI labs lock up capacity, some cloud providers are demanding multi-year contracts, prepayments of up to 30% of contract value and even payment guarantors. Startups must decide whether to buy too much compute and risk wasting cash if user growth disappoints, or buy too little and miss growth opportunities. That has created a business of global compute prospecting: finding underused AI server resources and renting them out. San Francisco Compute, a representative company, has collected servers from old chicken coops in rural America, and Musk has discussed further compute cooperation with TSMC, according to QbitAI. Top Silicon Valley venture capital firms are also stockpiling GPUs. Y Combinator launched a dedicated GPU cluster for its startups in July, and Radical Ventures helps portfolio companies coordinate supplier contracts.

The shortage has complex causes. OpenAI, Meta and Google are all building new data centers and promising vast GPU resources in the future, but model demand cannot wait for that capacity to come online. The way users interact with AI is adding pressure. Since this year, agents have begun replacing single-turn question-and-answer interactions as a core usage pattern, forcing servers to handle more parallel computing for long-running tasks. Rental prices have moved accordingly. SemiAnalysis data published in April showed the one-year H100 rental contract price rose from a low of $1.70 per GPU per hour in October 2025 to $2.35 in March 2026, an increase of nearly 40%.

The result is a compute hierarchy. According to QbitAI, the narrative of startups challenging industry giants will fade because even a good roadmap is useless without enough computing resources. Compute is becoming an entry threshold for the AI era and reinforcing the advantages of large companies that own infrastructure. AI product companies face more variables: they must worry about whether anyone will use their products and whether user growth will outpace their compute expansion. The middle layer selling shovels is benefiting, the report said.
